---
title: "A Shiny project"
subtitle: "Every app starts as an RStudio project with two scripts"
---

A Shiny app is **a folder**. In the folder there are (at least) two R scripts:

- `ui.R`: what the user **sees** (the *User Interface*)
- `server.R`: what R **does** (the computations)

The best way to keep that folder tidy is an **RStudio project**.
RStudio has a specific type of project for Shiny apps, which comes with a ready-made (and pretty basic) app.

This project will also become the GitHub repository that, on Day 2, is uploaded to the server to make the app shareable and online.

## Step 1 · Create a Shiny project

In RStudio:

1. *File* → *New Project…* → *New Directory* → **Shiny Application**
2. **Directory name**: `my-shiny-app` (no spaces, no accents)
3. Choose where to save it (e.g., `Documents/GitHub`) and click *Create Project*

RStudio opens the project and the example app that comes with it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why a project?

- The project folder **is** the app: everything the app needs lives there
- File paths are relative to the project, so the app works on any computer
- On Day 2 the very same folder becomes a GitHub repository and then goes online
:::

## Step 2 · Check that you have `ui.R` and `server.R`

Look at the *Files* pane. Depending on the version of RStudio, the example app is either split into **`ui.R`** and **`server.R`**, or written in a single file called **`app.R`**.

- If you see `ui.R` and `server.R`: Go to Step 3 (@sec-step3)
- If you see `app.R`: delete it, then create the two scripts yourself: *File* → *New File* → *R Script*, save it (*File* → *Save*) as **`ui.R`**; do the same for **`server.R`**

The names must be **exactly** `ui.R` and `server.R` (lowercase, capital `R`), and both files must be in the same folder.

Your project now looks like this:

```text
my-shiny-app/
├── my-shiny-app.Rproj
├── ui.R
└── server.R
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Alternative: start from a regular project

You can obtain exactly the same result from a regular RStudio project:

1. *File* → *New Project…* → *New Directory* → *New Project*, call it `my-shiny-app` and click *Create Project*
2. *File* → *New File* → *R Script*, then save it as **`ui.R`**
3. *File* → *New File* → *R Script*, then save it as **`server.R`**

The folder is the same as above: what makes it a Shiny app are the two scripts, not the type of project.
:::

## Step 4 · Run the app

As soon as a file called `ui.R` or `server.R` is open, RStudio replaces the usual *Run* button with **▶ Run App**. Click it.

What happens:

1. In the console you read something like `Listening on http://127.0.0.1:4321`: R has started a small **web server** on your computer
2. A window (or a browser tab) opens with the app: that is the UI, turned into a web page
3. The console shows a red **stop** sign: **R is busy** serving the app, so you cannot use the console until you stop it

Choose another option in the menu: the text changes. Every time you change the input, the browser tells R, R runs the code in the server and sends back the new result.

To **stop** the app, click the red stop sign in the console (or press {{< kbd Esc >}} in the console). If you change the code while the app is running, click *Reload app* in the app window.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The most common problems at this stage

- **No *Run App* button** → the file is not saved, or it is not called exactly `ui.R`/`server.R`
- **`could not find function "fluidPage"`** → `library(shiny)` is missing, or shiny is not installed
- **The console does not respond** → the app is still running: stop it first
:::

## Two files or one file?

Shiny also accepts a single file called `app.R` that contains both pieces and ends with `shinyApp()`:

```r
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(...)                              # what was in ui.R
server <- function(input, output, session) {...}  # what was in server.R

shinyApp(ui, server)                              # put them together
```

It is the same app. We use two files because they make the logic visible: **one script for what the user sees, one for what R does**. On Day 2 we will add a tiny `app.R` that simply reads the two files, because that is what the online server looks for.

::: {.callout-tip}
